title: Majority of General Counsel Indicate Openness to Using AI in Nearly Every Major Legal Use Case, According to The General Counsel Report
author: FTI Consulting

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central account of rising in-house AI adoption constrained by organisational readiness: use is increasing, yet most departments lack technology roadmaps and feel poorly prepared for AI risks. Its finding of greater reliance on outside counsel tempers claims of near-term insourcing but is consistent with the cluster’s caution that buyer intentions have not yet produced market-wide transformation.
qs: Generative AI use has also increased over the past year, with 44% of general counsel saying their legal teams are now using generative AI, compared to 28% in 2024 and 20% in 2023.
- Even with widespread recognition of the value of technology, 75% of legal departments lack a technology roadmap, making it more difficult to plan and effectively allocate budget.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report supports selective, supervised legal-AI adoption rather than autonomous deployment. Its survey evidence shows rising use alongside severe preparedness and planning gaps, while its recommendations emphasize expert human oversight and use-case-specific experimentation. It does not address apprenticeship risks directly, but aligns with the cluster’s broader proposition that benefits depend on verification, user capability and organisational complements.
qs: - The report revealed a slight improvement in technology readiness — 85% of general counsel said they felt minimally or not at all prepared to face the risks of generative AI, down from 93% in 2024.

What we continue to see among our teams and clients is that traditional AI still has strong value in legal use cases, and at the same time, generative AI has tremendous potential to improve outcomes when applied with expert human oversight.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s core proposition that legal AI should be deployed selectively through expert-led testing and human oversight, rather than treating uptake as evidence of competence or value. Its survey findings on technology-assessment workloads and absent roadmaps also support the need for operating-model planning.
qs: What we continue to see among our teams and clients is that traditional AI still has strong value in legal use cases, and at the same time, generative AI has tremendous potential to improve outcomes when applied with expert human oversight.

kp.k: Evidence combines interviews and a multinational corporate counsel survey
kp.d: The March 26, 2025 release reports findings from two separate data pools collected in 2024: Ari Kaplan's interviews with 34 general counsel or chief legal officers in July and August, and Censuswide's September survey of 207 general counsel and chief legal officers. Among interviewees, 65% had global responsibilities and 63% worked in organizations with more than $500 million in annual revenue. Survey respondents worked in organizations with more than $100 million in annual revenue and more than 1,000 employees across four regions.
qs: In July and August 2024, Ari Kaplan personally interviewed 34 leaders serving as the general counsel or chief legal officer of their organizations.
Sixty-five percent have a role with global responsibilities, and 63% work in organizations with more than $500 million in annual revenue.

Separately, in September 2024, Censuswide conducted a quantitative survey of 207 general counsel and chief legal officers at organizations with more than $100 million in annual revenue and more than 1,000 employees in South America, North America, Europe and Asia Pacific.

kp.k: Reported generative AI adoption rises across annual editions
kp.d: The report states that 44% of general counsel said their legal teams used generative AI, compared with 28% in the 2024 edition and 20% in 2023. Separately, more than two-thirds expressed interest in departmental use; interest and reported adoption are distinct findings.
qs: More than two-thirds of general counsel have expressed interest in using generative artificial intelligence within the legal department
Generative AI use has also increased over the past year, with 44% of general counsel saying their legal teams are now using generative AI, compared to 28% in 2024 and 20% in 2023.

kp.k: Technology investment plans include generative AI implementations
kp.d: Approximately 65% of legal departments planned new technology investment in the year ahead, with 30% of that group listing generative AI for upcoming implementation. Other planned purchases or improvements concerned contract lifecycle management, enterprise legal management, matter management and automation. These are stated plans rather than completed implementations.
qs: Alongside growing interest in AI within legal, approximately 65% of legal departments plan to invest in new technology in the year ahead, and 30% of that group have generative AI on their list for upcoming implementations.

In addition to plans to purchase or improve the use of tools spanning contract lifecycle management, enterprise legal management, matter management and automation, legal department leaders expressed high comfort levels using generative AI for legal use cases including legal research, e-discovery, document review, contract analysis and more.

kp.k: Comfort varies across legal tasks and regions
kp.d: The release reports high comfort with generative AI in legal research, e-discovery, document review and contract analysis, but investigations attracted the lowest comfort: 47% rated openness at one or two on a five-point scale. For AI in e-discovery, Latin American respondents were most comfortable, with 86% open to use, compared with 55% in Asia Pacific, the least comfortable region.
qs: General counsel in Latin America were the most likely to be comfortable with the use of AI in e-discovery, with 86% open to it, compared to only 55% in Asia Pacific, which was the least comfortable with it.

General counsel are least comfortable with the use of generative AI in investigations, with 47% rating their openness at a one or two on a scale of one (not at all comfortable) to five (extremely comfortable).

kp.k: Technology evaluation adds workload amid weak planning
kp.d: The report finds that 75% of respondents experienced increased workloads from evaluating new technologies for their organizations. Separately, 75% of legal departments lacked a technology roadmap, which the release describes as making planning and effective budget allocation more difficult.
qs: Most respondents (75%) have experienced an increase in workloads related to evaluating new technologies for their organization.
Even with widespread recognition of the value of technology, 75% of legal departments lack a technology roadmap, making it more difficult to plan and effectively allocate budget.

kp.k: Most counsel remain unprepared for generative AI risks
kp.d: Despite a reported improvement, 85% of general counsel felt minimally or not at all prepared to face generative AI risks, down from 93% in 2024. This finding concerns self-reported preparedness, rather than measured ability to manage risks.
qs: The report revealed a slight improvement in technology readiness — 85% of general counsel said they felt minimally or not at all prepared to face the risks of generative AI, down from 93% in 2024.

kp.k: Outside counsel reliance grows with risk and demand
kp.d: Increased reliance on law firms was the most popular reported response to increasing risk and escalating demand, with 79% of general counsel turning to outside counsel more frequently. The finding is presented as a broader response to departmental pressures, not as an effect specifically attributed to AI.
qs: Increased reliance on law firms was the most popular strategy general counsel cited for addressing increasing risk and escalating demand, with 79% confirming they turn to outside counsel more frequently.

kp.k: Ross conditions AI benefits on expert human oversight
kp.d: FTI Technology's Sophie Ross describes growing exploration of AI for efficiency and effectiveness, while emphasizing concerns about viability, availability, reliability and cost. She asserts that traditional AI retains value and that generative AI has potential to improve outcomes with expert human oversight, recommending expert-led testing and experimentation. These are her assessments and recommendations, rather than quantified findings of improved outcomes.
qs: However, this increasing comfort level must be balanced against an assortment of persistent concerns, including the technology’s viability, availability, reliability and cost.

What we continue to see among our teams and clients is that traditional AI still has strong value in legal use cases, and at the same time, generative AI has tremendous potential to improve outcomes when applied with expert human oversight.

The findings in *The General Counsel Report* confirm that the legal field is feeling the effects of active technological disruption, and legal departments must continue to pursue expert-led testing and experimentation to understand the applications that will make the most impact for their needs.

kp.k: Horrigan interprets adoption growth as legal transformation
kp.d: Relativity's David Horrigan interprets the findings as confirming that generative AI is a fundamentally transformative technology reshaping legal practice rather than a passing fad. He supports that characterization by pointing to reported adoption rising from less than one-third in the previous edition to 44% in 2025; the transformative characterization is his interpretation of the data.
qs: namely that generative AI is not a flash-in-the-pan fad, but rather a fundamentally transformative technology that is reshaping the practice of law

Last year, less than a third of general counsel said their teams were using generative AI, but that figure jumped to 44% in the 2025 report, underscoring that generative AI is an important technology for the legal profession and its chief legal officers.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The report presents rising generative AI adoption and broad openness among corporate legal departments; its quoted executives describe transformative potential subject to human oversight and persistent practical concerns.
pts.d: FTI Consulting and Relativity report that 44% of general counsel say their teams use generative AI, compared with 28% in the 2024 report and 20% in 2023. More than two-thirds express interest in departmental use. Approximately 65% of departments plan new technology investment, and 30% of that group list generative AI for implementation; the latter is not 30% of all departments. The source identifies comfort with legal research, e-discovery, document review and contract analysis, while investigations attract greater reservations. Sophie Ross, FTI Technology's Global Chief Executive Officer, says general counsel are exploring efficiency and effectiveness gains, traditional AI retains value, and generative AI has potential to improve outcomes with expert human oversight. David Horrigan, Relativity's Discovery Counsel and Legal Education Director, characterizes generative AI as fundamentally transforming legal practice. These executive interpretations go beyond the reported adoption and attitude measures.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of executive interviews and a separate quantitative survey, supplemented by attributed practitioner interpretations.
pts.d: Ari Kaplan interviewed 34 general counsel or chief legal officers in July and August 2024. Sixty-five percent had global responsibilities and 63% worked at organizations with annual revenue above $500 million. Censuswide separately surveyed 207 general counsel and chief legal officers in September 2024 at organizations with revenue above $100 million and more than 1,000 employees across four regions. The release compares adoption and risk-readiness figures with prior report editions but does not specify whether the same respondents were followed. These are reported use, intentions, comfort and preparedness measures, rather than measured productivity or legal-outcome results. Ross additionally invokes experience with teams and clients. Horrigan uses the adoption increase to support his interpretation of enduring transformation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The March 2025 release reports evidence collected in 2024, prospective investment intentions, and conditional rather than demonstrated outcome improvements.
pts.d: Published March 26, 2025, the release labels findings as the 2025 report, although interviews and survey responses were collected in July–September 2024. Adoption comparisons refer to the 2023, 2024 and 2025 report editions. Technology purchases are planned for 'the year ahead'; the release does not give precise implementation dates. Ross conditions generative AI's potential benefits on expert human oversight and calls for expert-led testing and experimentation. She identifies viability, availability, reliability and cost as continuing concerns. Risk preparedness remains limited: 85% report being minimally or not at all prepared, compared with 93% in the 2024 report. No deadline is supplied for the broader transformation predicted by the executives.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected group is large corporate legal departments and their leaders, with differences by task and region and continuing reliance on outside counsel.
pts.d: The source concerns the corporate buyer side: general counsel, chief legal officers and legal teams evaluating and implementing technology. It reports greater workload from evaluating new technologies for 75% of respondents and a lack of technology roadmaps in 75% of departments; these findings concern technology broadly, not solely AI. Openness to AI in e-discovery is 86% in Latin America versus 55% in Asia Pacific. Investigations are the least comfortable generative AI use case, with 47% rating openness one or two on a five-point scale. Outside law firms remain important: 79% report turning to outside counsel more frequently to address increasing risk and demand. The release does not establish that AI causes that increased reliance, or predict lawyer displacement, staffing changes or pricing changes.
